stem: A 72-year-old woman has an inferior wall myocardial infarction. Angiography shows a left-dominant coronary circulation and a tight narrowing in the artery that supplies the diaphragmatic surface of the heart and the AV node.
oneliner: 72F + inferior MI + left-dominant circulation + narrowed artery supplies diaphragmatic surface and AV node → which artery?

whyNot.A: Supplies the inferior wall in the **85% right-dominant** hearts; here the angiogram shows **left dominance**
whyNot.B: Supplies the **anterior wall and anterior septum**, not the diaphragmatic surface
whyNot.D: A branch of the right coronary artery to the **right ventricle**; in a **left-dominant** heart it does not feed the diaphragmatic surface or AV node
whyNot.E: A branch of the LAD to the **anterolateral wall**, not the diaphragmatic surface

why: **Dominance is set by the origin of the posterior descending artery.** In the right-dominant majority (about **85%**) it comes from the **RCA**; in **left dominance** it comes from the **circumflex**, so that vessel feeds the inferior wall and AV node.

idea.rule: Dominance = which artery gives the posterior descending artery.
also: Right dominant (~85%): RCA gives the PDA
Co-dominant: PDA branches from both RCA and circumflex
RCA also supplies the SA node in most people
Inferior MI with heart block suggests the artery giving the AV nodal branch

stem: A 60-year-old woman has chest pain with inferior ST elevation. She then develops raised neck veins, hepatomegaly and ascites. Her lung fields are clear.
oneliner: 60F + inferior ST elevation + raised neck veins + hepatomegaly + ascites + clear lungs → which artery?
ask: Occlusion of which artery most likely explains these findings?

whyNot.A: Anterior wall and septum infarct causes **left heart failure with pulmonary edema**, not clear lungs with venous congestion
whyNot.B: Gives **lateral wall** infarction and does not supply the right ventricle, so it would not explain **raised neck veins with clear lungs**
whyNot.C: Would produce **massive anterior and lateral** infarction with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema
whyNot.D: Small LAD branch to the **anterolateral wall**; no right-sided failure

why: The **right ventricle** is supplied by the **RCA** (marginal branches), and **inferior ST elevation** points to the same vessel. A failing right ventricle gives **high venous pressure with clear lungs**.

idea.rule: Inferior MI plus clear lungs and high JVP = RV infarct = RCA.
also: Treat RV infarct with fluids and avoid nitrates and diuretics
RCA occlusion can also cause bradycardia or AV block
Left-sided failure gives crackles; right-sided failure gives clear lungs

stem: A 25-year-old man who is tall with long fingers has upward subluxation of both lenses and a diastolic murmur along the left sternal border. Genetic testing shows a fibrillin-1 mutation, and echocardiography shows a dilated aorta.
oneliner: 25M + tall + long fingers + upward lens subluxation + diastolic murmur + fibrillin-1 mutation + dilated aorta → which segment?
ask: Which segment of the aorta is dilated?

whyNot.A: Site of **atherosclerotic** aneurysm in older smokers; it would not cause the **diastolic murmur** of aortic regurgitation
whyNot.B: Typical site of **traumatic tears** and atherosclerotic disease; dilating it would not cause **aortic regurgitation**
whyNot.C: Arch dilation does not stretch the **valve ring**, so it would not give the **diastolic murmur**
whyNot.E: An uncommon aneurysm site far from the valve; it cannot explain the **diastolic murmur**

why: **Fibrillin-1** deficiency weakens elastic fibers, causing **cystic medial degeneration** of the **aortic root and ascending aorta**. This produces **aortic regurgitation** and risk of dissection.

idea.rule: Marfan dilates the proximal aorta (root); atherosclerosis dilates the infrarenal abdominal aorta.
also: Syphilitic aortitis also dilates the ascending aorta (tree-bark intima)
Bicuspid aortic valve is linked to ascending aortic dilation
Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGF-beta receptor) also dilates the aortic root

stem: A 58-year-old man has chest pain, ST elevation in leads V4 to V6 and new lateral Q waves.
oneliner: 58M + chest pain + ST elevation V4-V6 + new lateral Q waves → which wall and artery?
ask: Which wall and artery are involved?

options.C: Left circumflex or diagonal branch (anterolateral wall)

whyNot.A: Inferior MI shows ST elevation in **II, III and aVF**, not V4-V6
whyNot.B: Also an **inferior** territory with II, III, aVF changes
whyNot.D: Right ventricular infarct shows **right-sided leads and raised JVP**, not lateral precordial leads
whyNot.E: Anteroseptal MI shows changes in **V1-V2**, not V4-V6

answer: Anterolateral wall: LAD diagonal or left circumflex
why: **V4-V6** look at the **anterolateral wall of the left ventricle**, supplied by the **diagonal branches of the LAD and the left circumflex**. Inferior and right ventricular infarcts show their changes in other leads.

idea.rule: Lead group gives the wall: V1-V2 septal, V3-V4 anterior, V4-V6 anterolateral, I/aVL/V5-V6 lateral, II/III/aVF inferior.
also: Inferior MI (II, III, aVF): usually the RCA
Anteroseptal MI (V1-V2): the LAD
Lateral MI (I, aVL, V5-V6): the left circumflex

stem: A 24-year-old soldier has a piece of shrapnel protruding from the lower sternum, lodged just behind the bone at the level of the 3rd to 5th intercostal spaces.
oneliner: 24M + shrapnel at lower sternum, behind the bone at 3rd-5th spaces → which heart chamber is hit first?
ask: Which cardiac chamber is most likely injured first?

whyNot.A: The most **posterior** chamber, lying against the esophagus, so it is protected from a front wound
whyNot.B: Forms the **left and apical** border; lies behind and to the left of the right ventricle
whyNot.C: Forms the **right border** of the heart and lies to the right of the sternum, higher up
whyNot.D: Lies **deep and superior**, behind the right ventricular outflow, not behind the lower sternum

why: The **right ventricle** is the most **anterior** chamber, lying directly behind the **lower sternum** and the **3rd to 5th spaces**. It also forms part of the **diaphragmatic surface** with the left ventricle.

idea.rule: Front of the heart = right ventricle; back of the heart = left atrium.
also: A parasternal heave at the left sternal border suggests right ventricular enlargement
Left atrium enlargement can compress the esophagus
Right atrium forms the right heart border

stem: A 17-year-old girl has dyspnea. She has a systolic murmur loudest at the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line, which radiates to the axilla.
oneliner: 17F + dyspnea + systolic murmur at left 5th space midclavicular line + radiates to axilla → which valve lesion?
ask: Which valve lesion is most likely?

whyNot.A: Systolic murmur at the **right second space** radiating to the carotids
whyNot.B: Heard at the **left lower sternal border** and louder on inspiration
whyNot.C: Heard at the **left upper sternal border** with an ejection click
whyNot.E: A **diastolic** rumble after an opening snap, not a systolic murmur

why: The **mitral valve** is heard best at the **apex**. A **systolic** murmur there radiating to the **axilla** is **mitral regurgitation**; mitral stenosis is **diastolic**.

also: Aortic area: right second space
Pulmonic area: left second space
Tricuspid area: left lower sternal border

stem: A 43-year-old man had a single heart valve replaced 10 years ago. On a lateral chest film, the prosthetic ring lies above a line drawn from the carina to the cardiac apex, in the middle of the heart shadow and well behind the anterior chest wall.
oneliner: 43M + prosthetic valve ring on lateral film + above the carina-to-apex line + central, well behind the anterior chest wall → which valve?

whyNot.C: Lies above the line but at the **front**, just behind the anterior chest wall
whyNot.D: Lies **below** the carina-apex line and anteriorly
whyNot.E: A small flap at the IVC opening, low in the right atrium and **below** the line; it is not replaced

why: On a lateral film, the **aortic and pulmonic** valves lie **above** the carina-apex line and the **mitral and tricuspid** below. The **aortic** valve is **posterior** and to the right of the pulmonic valve.

idea.rule: Above the carina-apex line: aortic (posterior) and pulmonic (anterior); below: mitral and tricuspid.
also: Mitral valve is posterior to tricuspid below the line
Pulmonic valve is the most anterior and superior
Prosthetic valve rings are radiopaque

stem: A 48-year-old man with right renal artery stenosis has a stent placed through femoral access. The guide wire is advanced up the abdominal aorta toward the renal arteries.
oneliner: 48M + renal artery stent via femoral access + wire advanced up the aorta → last branch passed before the renal arteries?
ask: Which aortic branch does the wire pass just before it reaches the renal arteries?

whyNot.A: Arises at **T12**, above the renal arteries, so the wire reaches it after them
whyNot.B: Arises at **L1**, above the renal arteries, so the wire reaches it after them
whyNot.D: Arises at **L3**; the wire passes it earlier, below the gonadal arteries
whyNot.E: Arises at the **iliac bifurcation**; it is the first branch region, not the last before the renals

why: The gonads develop in the **abdomen** and descend, so the **gonadal arteries** arise **high from the aorta, just below the renals** (L2). Order: **celiac, SMA, renals, gonadals, IMA**.

idea.rule: Gonads descend, so their arteries arise high, just below the renals.
also: Left testicular vein drains to the left renal vein
Right gonadal vein drains to the IVC
Celiac T12, SMA L1, renals L1-L2, IMA L3

stem: A 70-year-old man who smokes has sudden back pain and hypotension. Examination shows a pulsatile abdominal mass.
oneliner: 70M + smoker + sudden back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass → which aortic segment?
ask: Which aortic segment is most likely involved?

options.A: Suprarenal aorta at the celiac trunk

whyNot.A: Uncommon site; aneurysms in **older male smokers** favor the segment **below** the renal arteries
whyNot.B: Dilates in **Marfan syndrome and syphilis**, not as a pulsatile abdominal mass
whyNot.C: Would present with **chest or interscapular** pain, not an abdominal mass
whyNot.D: Isolated iliac aneurysms are less common and sit lower than a **pulsatile abdominal mass** in an older smoker usually lies

why: **Atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysms** form **below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation**, in **older male smokers**. **Sudden back pain with hypotension** suggests rupture.

idea.rule: Atherosclerotic aneurysm = abdominal, infrarenal; connective tissue disease = root.
also: Risk factors include smoking, male sex and age
Screen men 65-75 who ever smoked with ultrasound
Syphilis affects the ascending aorta

stem: A 65-year-old woman in hemorrhagic shock is having a central line placed in the right internal jugular vein.
oneliner: 65F + hemorrhagic shock + right internal jugular line placement → which structures at risk?
ask: Which structures are most at risk from a misplaced needle?

options.C: Common carotid artery and pulmonary artery
options.D: Common carotid artery and apex of the lung

whyNot.A: Neither lies near the **neck insertion site**; the pulmonary artery is deep in the chest
whyNot.B: The esophagus is **medial and deep** in the neck, not at the needle track
whyNot.C: The pulmonary artery lies far **below** the neck
whyNot.E: The esophagus is **deep and medial**, not along the needle path

answer: Common carotid artery and apex of the lung
why: The **internal jugular vein** lies **lateral to the common carotid artery** in the **carotid sheath**, and the **pleural dome** sits just below. A misplaced needle can therefore cause **carotid puncture or pneumothorax**.

idea.rule: Neck lines risk the carotid artery (medial) and the pleural dome (below).
also: Subclavian lines risk pneumothorax more than internal jugular lines
Ultrasound guidance lowers carotid puncture
Internal jugular vein lies lateral to the carotid

stem: A 41-year-old woman has hypertension, and renal vein sampling shows high renin from one kidney. A physician reviews where the angiotensin I produced in response is converted to the active vasoconstrictor.
oneliner: 41F + hypertension + high renal vein renin from one kidney + angiotensin I made → where is angiotensin II made?
ask: At which site is angiotensin I converted to angiotensin II?

whyNot.B: They **release renin**, which makes angiotensin I; they do not convert it
whyNot.C: The site that **senses low pressure** and holds the juxtaglomerular cells
whyNot.D: Responds to angiotensin II by **releasing aldosterone**; it does not make it

why: **ACE** on **pulmonary capillary endothelium** converts **angiotensin I** to **angiotensin II**. The kidney supplies renin, the liver supplies angiotensinogen, and the adrenal responds with aldosterone.

idea.rule: Liver makes angiotensinogen, kidney makes renin, lung makes angiotensin II.
also: ACE also breaks down bradykinin, causing cough with ACE inhibitors
Renal artery stenosis raises renin
Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole

stem: In a study of healthy women, a higher baseline plasma level of C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, predicts later coronary artery disease.
oneliner: Study of healthy women + raised CRP predicts coronary disease → which organ makes CRP?

whyNot.B: Is a **target** of inflammation but does not produce CRP
whyNot.D: Filters blood and holds **lymphoid tissue**; not the source of acute-phase proteins
whyNot.E: Is the site of **inflammation**, not the main source of CRP

why: **CRP** is an **acute-phase reactant** made by **hepatocytes** under **IL-6** stimulation. A raised level marks **vascular inflammation** and predicts **coronary disease**.

idea.rule: Acute-phase proteins come from the liver in response to IL-6.
also: Other acute-phase reactants: fibrinogen, ferritin, hepcidin, serum amyloid A
Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant
IL-1 and TNF-alpha also trigger the response
